Latin.note: The Greek temple-precinct assault is not explicitly expressed in this Latin interval; Hyrcanus’s retreat and detention of the family survive.
Greek §85 additionally describes prisoners taken. This Latin interval explicitly retains the three thousand killed, with no separate capture count here.
The oath and concealed beam survive in this Latin interval; the explicit statement that Eleazar alone knew the secret is not separately expressed here.
The Latin shortens the statement about sacred public money; the eight hundred talents and contextual inference survive.
The Latin compresses the ethnarch’s administrative functions to a short description of the ruler.
The Latin retains the Memphis response and subsequent visit across a paragraph boundary. Greek §132’s separate statement that the preceding group obeyed is not explicitly expressed here.

The approved boundary interpretation leaves tractaretque here as the concluding verb associated with Phasael’s handling of populi negotia. Antipatrum begins the following faciebat … honorari construction at162. The difficult wording and punctuation are preserved; see162.

The approved boundary begins before antipatrum, faciebat, retaining Antipatrum with the following faciebat … honorari construction. Tractaretque remains in161 as the concluding verb associated with Phasael’s handling of populi negotia. The comma after antipatrum and the difficult syntax are preserved. The later affirmative hyrcani fidem transgressus est differs from the Greek denial of disloyalty: no negative has been supplied. This interval must not be read as unqualified semantic equivalence.
Greek’s opening description of Hyrcanus’s inattention and the leaders’ fear is compressed out; the explicit charge survives.
The Latin departure and later-summons decision survive. The transmitted oboediret lacks the Greek section’s negation; it is preserved without emendation.
The rejoicing and expectation of increased profit survive. The Greek comparative assertion about greater injustice to others is not separately expressed in this compressed Latin interval.
The Latin annual-payment clause names ioppenses as paying Jerusalem; Greek §202 excludes Joppa from the Jerusalem payment. The Latin wording and the sabbatical exception are preserved.
The tithe to Hyrcanus and his sons survives. The Greek Sidon second-year quarter-of-seed provision is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.

The Jewish-association exception survives. The transmitted non prohibuit nec ... parare iussit does not separately reproduce Greek’s full paired exception for contributions and shared meals; no wording is supplied.
Subiugo etiam preserves the introduction of the appended decree. Greek’s explanatory purpose and final as-follows formula are compressed out here.
The Latin collective uel reliquo senatu replaces the continuation of the named-witness list. It supplies collective correspondence; the individual Greek §220 names are not reproduced.

The resolution of Dolabella and Antony survives. Greek §221’s preceding final witness Publius Serrius is not individually expressed in this shortened Latin list; the displayed interval begins with the consuls.
The collective Senate-presence formula replaces the detailed witnesses in Greek §229. Its individual names are not supplied here. Balgus begins the distinct salutation assigned to §230.

Text corresponding to Niese §238 is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The detailed witness list has no identifiable counterpart between the surviving exemption and date in §237 and Lentulus’s decree notice in §240. The cause is unknown.

Text corresponding to Niese §239 is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The detailed witness list has no identifiable counterpart between the surviving exemption and date in §237 and Lentulus’s decree notice in §240. The cause is unknown.
Prytanis’s complaint and the customary harvest reference survive. Greek’s expressly named sabbath and ancestral-rites restrictions are compressed to the Latin’s general inquietudinem.
The hearing and decision survive. The Latin ends with ne prohiberentur, without separately expressing Greek’s final object concerning customary practices.
The request for a decree copy and envoys, and to preserve and increase friendship, survives. Greek’s final become-a-cause-of-good phrase is not separately expressed here.
The Abraham-era friendship recollection survives. Greek’s preceding reciprocity-of-reward phrase is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
The grant for sabbaths and sacrifices, and the penalty for obstruction, survive. Greek’s shore-prayer clause is not separately expressed here.
The proconsul’s concession and people’s general permission survive. The Latin abbreviates Greek’s explicit sabbath-day and fine prohibitions; its transmitted nullum diem is preserved.
The lifting of the siege, recruitment and taxation survive. The Latin transmits LXX talents where the Greek gives seven hundred; no numeral is corrected.
Antipater’s division of the levy survives. The Latin names Herod where the Greek distribution additionally singles out Malichus; the transmitted wording remains unchanged.
The condolence and instruction to Herod survive. Latin names Cassius as the sender where the Greek account refers to Herod sending instructions; the wording is preserved independently.
The journey to Tyre survives. Latin continues with Herod as subject where the Greek narrative identifies Malichus; the transmitted subject sequence is retained without correction.
Marion’s occupation and Herod response survive. The Greek detailed recovery and release of the garrison are compressed in the Latin account.
Vengeance and the stronghold survive. The Greek detailed battle killings are compressed in the short Latin passage.
The reply and advance survive. Greek341’s explicit urging by Herod to attack and description of the arrivals are not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
The distrust and palace conversation survive. The difficult Latin fratrem adiuuare differs from the Greek argument about endangering the brother; no wording is supplied or corrected.
Herod distrust and the warnings of the women survive. The Latin describes betrothal to Hyrcanus’s daughter where the Greek specifies his daughter’s daughter; the transmitted relationship is retained.
Hyrcanus and Phasael among the prisoners survive. The Greek description of Herod’s young children and the friends held captive is shortened here.

Partial/reordered correspondence: closing material of Greek XIV.357 survives physically within the following Latin interval, at culis liberans, amatos traderet inimicis, completing the interrupted peri … culis. See XIV.358. The surviving tail is not absent; no cause of the disorder is inferred.

Partial/reordered correspondence: the first surviving counterpart of Greek XIV.358 begins Quibus uerbis compulsus facinus quod in se. It is interrupted by culis liberans, amatos traderet inimicis, the surviving closing material of XIV.357 completing peri … culis. XIV.358’s own construction resumes at cognitauerat pretermisit. This Latin interval includes displaced357 material and supplies only partial correspondence to358; wording has not been joined or moved.
The battle site and later foundation of Herodium survive. The Greek preceding description of defeating assailants along the route is compressed.
The Parthian plunder and spared Hyrcanus money survive. The amount reaches trecenta in Latin without an explicit talents unit here.

The Herod escape clause and devastation survive. The Latin transmits mulieres and the difficult Ille magis quae deportauerat where the Greek refers to Herod’s property; these words are preserved without reconstruction.
Phasael’s courage and self-inflicted death survive. Greek’s final denial of satisfaction to the enemy is not separately expressed in this shortened Latin interval.
Herod’s calamities and appeal to Malchus survive. Latin perterruit lacks the Greek negative; the independent wording is preserved.
The ransom project and child as pledge survive. Latin triginta talents differs from Greek three hundred; neither witness is rewritten.
Departure toward Egypt and hearing of Phasael’s death survive. The Greek notice of many followers left at the sanctuary is compressed.
The voyage to Rhodes and meeting of two friends survive. Greek’s explicit loss of cargo is not separately expressed here.

Distributed/reordered correspondence: quem postea interfecit, quod apto tempore referemus, the relative clause concerning the young man’s later death, survives here and corresponds to Greek XIV.388. It remains in the preserved Latin sequence before the subsequent seven-day passage corresponding to Greek XIV.387. See the reciprocal notice at388; no cause of the different ordering is inferred.

Distributed/reordered correspondence: the death reference of Greek XIV.388 survives earlier within the Latin interval for387, at quem postea interfecit, quod apto tempore referemus. This interval begins with senatu uero dimisso, the senate’s dismissal and ensuing procession. The death reference is not absent and has not been moved, duplicated or rewritten; see387.
The pacification, bribery and growing Herod force survive. Latin runs from Ventidius to the bribed man without Greek’s separately expressed Silo subject; no name is supplied.
Herod’s rescue of Silo and capture of Joppa survive. Greek’s explicit departure pretext and pursuit are compressed in the Latin introductory syntax.
Antigonus’s ambushes survive. The Greek opening statement about the large force assembled is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.

Latin conjoins multi fortitudinem eius with castraque ad occidentalem partem, so the local-reaction construction continues physically inside401 at cernentes metuerunt. The camp words open the401 counterpart; no syntax is repaired.

The western camp opens this Latin interval. The conjoined local-reaction construction from400 continues at cernentes metuerunt within401. The Greek camp and guards material survives with compressed and reordered syntax; see400.

Antigonus’s second entitlement argument survives in compressed and changed Latin syntax. Its phrasing about the priests and wrongdoing differs from Greek; no negation is corrected or extra reasoning supplied.

The provisioning expedition and supplies survive. Latin compresses the Samaria instruction as actual administration/transport and transmits per sex diebus where Greek concerns the following days; the wording is preserved.

The Jericho expedition survives. Latin describes five Jewish and five hired formations where Greek describes Roman/Jewish formations plus mixed mercenaries; the independent troop descriptions remain unchanged.
Herod’s dispatch and journey survive. Latin duobus militibus differs from Greek two thousand infantry; the numeral is retained.
Arrival at Sepphoris and abundant provisions survive. The Greek snowfall notice is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
Antony in Athens and the orders survive. The next Latin clause does not separately name Ventidius, who is explicitly identified in Greek; no name is supplied.

The fire-throwing belongs to428. Latin places the wood reference in circuitu siluae before the burning effect at429, whereas Greek429 explains the wood within its burning-caves account. All words retain their transmitted positions.

Latin starts with the burning effect et ita multos incenderunt and then the old man episode. The wood reference corresponding to Greek429 occurs earlier in the Latin interval assigned to428. See428; this is surviving reordered correspondence, not absence.

The cave-conquest conclusion continues into the next paragraph at Igitur his actis iam omnes speluncas obtinuerat rex, despite its inherited431 label. The actual431 cut follows at ubi ducem ptolomeum; visible labels remain unchanged.

The inherited XV.vi.431 label precedes the closing cave-conquest statement of Greek430. This section begins at ubi ducem ptolomeum. The visible inherited label is retained and its false early executable claim is suppressed; see430.
Recovery of the spoils survives. The Greek renewed statement of continued killing is compressed in the Latin transition.

Joseph’s head and the disturbances survive. Latin says Pheroras redeemed the head and Machaeras captured a strong fort, differing from Greek’s ransom offer and fortification statement; no words are changed.
Shelter in houses and removal of roofs survive. Greek’s detailed crowded-room observation is compressed before the stone-crushing interval460.

Stone crushing survives at lapidibus eos oppressit. Greek460’s extended spectacle of bodies piled on one another is not separately expressed in this short Latin interval. This is partial correspondence, not whole-section absence.
The naked king and passing armed men survive. Greek’s explanation of the men’s fear and satisfaction at escaping unharmed is compressed.
The next-day severed head and vengeance survive. Latin makes Pheroras send it to Herod, while the Greek wording makes Herod send it to Pheroras; the transmitted roles remain unchanged.

The defenders’ undaunted resistance and burning equipment survive. The transmitted non minores romani fuerunt wording differs from Greek’s comparison of the defenders with the Romans; it is preserved.
The killings and Roman resentment survive. Latin names Herod directly where Greek refers to the Jewish force around Herod; no subject is supplied or rewritten.
